screens.title: Setting Up the Node.js Fabric SDK Environment
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will prepare a practical Node. js environment for building Hyperledger Fabric client applications. You will learn which system prerequisites matter, how to initialize a Node. js project, which Hyperledger Fabric npm packages to install, and how to use a common connection profile so your client can talk to a running test-network. This setup is the foundation for every Fabric application: correct Node and npm versions avoid runtime incompatibilities, the package manifest keeps dependencies reproducible, and the connection profile tells the SDK where peers, orderers, and certificate authorities live. As a concrete example, we will load the provided connection-org1. json into a small app, initialize a Wallet, and attempt a Gateway connection. Expect to see an expected message that an application identity is missing, which confirms you loaded the profile correctly. Finally, I'll point out two frequent mistakes — wrong file paths for TLS certificates and a stopped Fabric network — and show how verifying those resolves most connection failures. After this orientation, you'll be ready to create the project scaffolding and run the sample app.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Setting Up the Node.js Fabric SDK Environment
Setting Up the Node.js Fabric SDK Environment
Prepare your project, install core SDK packages, and make a basic Gateway connection.
In this lesson

Install Node.js and npm or use nvm; initialize package.json; install hyperledger-fabric-network and hyperledger-fabric-client; copy the connection profile and organizations directory; run a small app that loads the CCP and initializes the Gateway.

What you will be able to do

Verify Node and npm versions, produce a reproducible package.json, load a connection profile, create a filesystem wallet, and observe expected identity messages when a user is not yet enrolled.

Explore Key Topics
Prerequisites
Node.js, npm, and a version manager are required to avoid compatibility issues.
Connection Profile
A JSON or YAML blueprint describing peers, orderers, and certificate locations.
Gateway Init
Load the CCP, create a Wallet, and call gateway.connect with discovery settings.
Visual Concept
Client App
package.json, app.js, wallet, connection-org1.json
Network Artifacts
organizations/, peers, orderers, TLS certs
Quick note
Copy the connection profile and the organizations directory into your project so TLS paths in the CCP resolve correctly when parsed by the SDK.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives define practical outcomes you should achieve. First, you will identify and install the prerequisites required for Node. js Fabric development: a supported Node. js runtime and npm, and optionally a version manager such as nvm. This prevents runtime errors caused by version mismatches. Second, you will initialize and configure a Node. js project, create a package. json manifest, and add the core Hyperledger Fabric SDK packages so your code can import the Gateway and client utilities. Third, you will understand the structure of a common connection profile: how peers, orderers, certificate authorities, endpoints, and TLS certificate paths are represented. Knowing this structure helps you locate and fix path or endpoint errors. Fourth, you will establish a basic connection from a Node. js client to a running test-network by loading the CCP, creating a filesystem wallet, checking for an identity, and calling gateway. connect with discovery options. Each objective emphasizes the practical steps and why they matter. These skills let you reliably bootstrap new Fabric client projects and avoid common setup mistakes that block development.

screens.title: Prerequisites: Node.js, npm, and nvm
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable development environment starts with the correct runtime. Node. js and npm are required because the Fabric Node. js SDK is distributed as npm packages and depends on Node's event-driven model. Use a supported LTS version to avoid incompatibilities; many Fabric SDKs are tested against recent LTS releases. To verify your environment, run the terminal checks that show the installed versions. If your version is out of range, a version manager such as nvm is a practical solution. It lets you install and switch between Node versions without interfering with system packages. For example, you might keep one LTS version for Fabric work and a different version for other projects. A common misconception is that any Node version will work; in practice, mismatched Node versions produce runtime errors or native module build failures. Another pitfall is global package pollution; prefer local project dependencies declared in package. json. Concrete example: run node -v and npm -v, then install nvm and use it to install Node 18 if your system runs an older release. Key takeaway: consistent Node and npm versions remove a large class of setup failures and make team environments reproducible.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Prerequisites: Node.js, npm, and nvm
What to install
  • Node.js runtime (use an LTS release used by Fabric SDKs).
  • npm, bundled with Node, used to install SDK packages into your project.
  • nvm is optional but recommended for managing multiple Node versions safely.
Example commands
node -v // check runtime
npm -v // check package manager
Common mistake
Assuming any Node version will work. If your Node version is unsupported by the SDK you may see subtle runtime failures or native module errors.
Why this matters
Fabric SDKs are regular Node packages and depend on Node behavior. Ensuring the correct Node and npm versions prevents dependency and runtime issues while developing and running client code.
Concrete example
If your team standard is Node 18, use nvm to install and activate Node 18. Then run the same npm install commands so package-lock.json and node_modules are consistent across developers.
Key Takeaway

Pin and verify Node and npm versions early. Use local project dependencies to avoid global package conflicts.

screens.title: Initialize the Node.js project
screens.narratorSegment: Initializing a Node. js project produces the package. json manifest that records dependencies, scripts, and metadata. This file is critical because npm uses it to install required packages reproducibly across environments. Start by navigating to your desired project directory and running the initialization command which generates a minimal package. json. After initialization, install the core Fabric packages: hyperledger-fabric-network and hyperledger-fabric-client. Installing these populates package. json dependencies and creates node_modules. A common pitfall is installing packages globally instead of as project dependencies; global installs make it hard to reproduce the environment on other machines. Another issue is neglecting to check package-lock. json, which locks dependency versions and helps ensure that team members install the same package versions. Concrete example: run npm init -y, then npm install hyperledger-fabric-network hyperledger-fabric-client. After the install, open package. json and confirm the dependencies section includes the SDK packages. Key takeaway: a well-formed package. json and committed package-lock. json make team development reliable and repeatable. Initialize the Node.js project means npm init creates package.json; npm install adds the sdk packages locally and updates package.json and package-lock.json for reproducibility.. In practical terms, create package.json and prepare for sdk dependency installs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Initialize the Node.js project
Step-by-step
1. Create project folder and open terminal.
2. Run: npm init -y to generate package.json.
3. Run: npm install hyperledger-fabric-network hyperledger-fabric-client.
4. Inspect package.json and package-lock.json; commit them to source control.
Why package-lock.json matters
The lockfile records exact dependency tree versions. When teammates run an install, npm reads package-lock.json to produce identical node_modules, avoiding unexpected behavior caused by transitive dependency updates.
Pro tip
Prefer local installs and commit both package.json and package-lock.json to your repository to guarantee consistent installs in CI and on fellow developers' machines.

screens.title: Core SDK packages
screens.narratorSegment: Two primary npm packages drive Node. js Fabric clients. The higher-level package exposes the Gateway A P I and is intended for most application code. The lower-level package contains utilities and more granular APIs the higher-level package may use. Installing both ensures you can use the Gateway and, when necessary, access lower-level helpers. The hyperledger-fabric-network package simplifies interactions such as submitting transactions, listening for events, and handling endorsement logic. The hyperledger-fabric-client package provides additional constructs for building custom integrations. A misconception is that you only need the high-level package; in practice installing both is common because the network package may rely on client utilities and it ensures compatibility. Concrete example: after running the install command, your package. json will list both packages under dependencies and node_modules will contain their code and sub-dependencies. Key takeaway: include the network package for everyday Gateway-based code and the client package when deeper control or legacy utilities are required. Core SDK packages means use hyperledger-fabric-network for the gateway api and hyperledger-fabric-client for lower-level utilities and deeper integration points.. Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Core SDK packages
hyperledger-fabric-network
Provides the Gateway abstraction to connect, submit transactions, and manage contracts without handling low-level details.
Everyday app code should prefer this package to orchestrate proposal endorsements and submission flows.
hyperledger-fabric-client
Contains lower-level utilities and APIs sometimes needed for specialized operations or compatibility with legacy code paths.
Install alongside the network package to ensure required utilities are available and to match sample project expectations.
Example
npm install hyperledger-fabric-network hyperledger-fabric-client will add both packages to dependencies and create node_modules. Confirm package.json lists them under dependencies.

screens.title: Common Connection Profile (CCP)
screens.narratorSegment: A common connection profile is the client's blueprint for reaching the Fabric network. It is a JSON or YAML file that describes the network topology from the client perspective: which peers and orderers exist, how to reach them, which certificate authorities issue identities, channel information, and timeouts. Key fields include peers, orderers, certificateAuthorities, and client settings. Each peer and orderer entry contains a URL and a tlsCACerts reference that points to a TLS root certificate file. The CCP centralizes network endpoints so client code can simply load the profile instead of hardcoding addresses. A concrete example is a connection-org1. json that lists peer0. org1. example. com with a grpcs URL and a tlsCACerts. path pointing to a local file under organizations/peerOrganizations. A common misconception is that the CCP alone makes the network secure; the CCP points to TLS materials, but the client still needs correct certificate files and the right identity in a wallet. Key takeaway: inspect the CCP to confirm endpoint URLs and tlsCACerts paths are correct and resolvable from the client project's directory. Common Connection Profile (CCP) means the ccp describes endpoints, tls certificate locations, and ca settings so the sdk can discover and connect to fabric services without hardcoded addresses.. In practical terms, structure, purpose, and essential fields. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CCP purpose
keyIdea.text: The CCP describes endpoints, TLS certificate locations, and CA settings so the SDK can discover and connect to Fabric services without hardcoded addresses.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Common Connection Profile (CCP)
Essential CCP fields
  • peers: mapping of peer names to URLs and tlsCACerts paths.
  • orderers: mapping for ordering service endpoints and TLS certs.
  • certificateAuthorities: CA URLs and caName entries used for enrollment.
  • client: timeout and organization settings used by the SDK.
Readability tip
Open the CCP and search for tlsCACerts.path entries. Confirm those files exist relative to the CCP location or convert them to absolute paths if necessary. Consistency here avoids the most frequent connection failures.
Small CCP excerpt
{
  "peers": {
    "peer0.org1.example.com": {
      "url": "grpcs://localhost:7051",
      "tlsCACerts": {
        "path": "organizations/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/tls/ca.crt"
      }
    }
  }
}

screens.title: Relative vs Absolute Certificate Paths
screens.narratorSegment: TLS certificate paths referenced inside the CCP can be relative or absolute, and the SDK resolves those paths relative to where the CCP file is loaded. A common workflow is copying the connection-org1. json and the organizations directory into your project so the relative paths resolve directly. If you leave the CCP in another folder or run the app from a different working directory, relative paths may not be found and the SDK will fail to load TLS certificates, causing connection errors. An absolute path removes ambiguity but reduces portability between machines. A good compromise is to keep the CCP and organizations directory together inside the client project and use path. resolve in code to construct a reliable ccpPath before reading the file. Concrete example: copy the organizations directory into your project root so tlsCACerts. path entries like organizations/peerOrganizations/... refer to existing files. Misconception: TLS will work without those files. In truth, the SDK must load the root CA certificates to establish TLS connections. Key takeaway: ensure TLS cert file paths in the CCP point to resolvable files from your application's execution context.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Relative vs Absolute Certificate Paths
Relative paths
Paths like organizations/peerOrganizations/... are resolved relative to the CCP file location. Copy the organizations directory into your project to make these paths valid.
Advantage: portable when CCP and artifacts move together. Pitfall: broken if you run the app from a different working directory.
Absolute paths
Replacing relative paths with absolute paths removes ambiguity but ties the CCP to a machine-specific layout.
Use when you control the deployment environment, but prefer relative paths for shared code repositories.
Practical tip
Copy the CCP and organizations/ directory from fabric-samples/test-network into your project to keep relative tlsCACerts.path entries resolvable on local development machines.

screens.title: Bring up the test-network
screens.narratorSegment: Before attempting a Gateway connection, verify the Fabric test-network is running. The samples repository provides a network script that brings up peers, orderers, and certificate authorities. Use the command that creates a channel and enables certificate authorities so the network mirrors the artifacts referenced in connection-org1. json. If you try to connect while the network is down, you'll see connection refused errors because the SDK cannot reach the endpoints listed in the CCP. A concrete example is running the sample network script with the create channel and CA flags. After launching the network, check container logs or the script output to confirm peers and the orderer are healthy. Misconception: starting only some services is sufficient. In reality, missing any critical service referenced by the CCP will cause discovery or connection failures. Key takeaway: always verify the test-network is fully up and reachable before running client code, and match the organization used in the CCP with the artifacts you copied into the project. Bring up the test-network means the fabric network must be running and reachable for the sdk to connect; otherwise the client will receive connection refused errors.. In practical terms, ensure peers, orderers, and cas are running before connecting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Bring up the test-network
Checklist to start the network
  1. Change into fabric-samples/test-network.
  2. Run the network script to bring up peers and orderers and create a channel with certificate authorities enabled.
  3. Confirm containers are healthy using your container runtime or the script output.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › app.js code walkthrough
app.js (core excerpt)
// app.js
'use strict';

const { Gateway, Wallets } = require('hyperledger-fabric-network');
const path = require('path');
const fs = require('fs');

async function main() {
    try {
        const ccpPath = path.resolve(__dirname, 'connection-org1.json');
        const ccp = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(ccpPath, 'utf8'));

        const walletPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'wallet');
        const wallet = await Wallets.newFileSystemWallet(walletPath);
        console.log(`Wallet path: ${walletPath}`);

        const identity = await wallet.get('appUser');
        if (!identity) {
            console.log('An identity for the user "appUser" does not exist in the wallet');
            console.log('Run the enrollUser.js application before retrying');
            return;
        }

        const gateway = new Gateway();
        await gateway.connect(ccp, { wallet, identity: 'appUser', discovery: { enabled: true, asLocalhost: true } });

        console.log('Successfully connected to the Fabric network Gateway.');
        await gateway.disconnect();
        console.log('Disconnected from the Fabric network Gateway.');

    } catch (error) {
        console.error(`Failed to connect to the Fabric network: ${error}`);
        process.exit(1);
    }
}

main();
Explanation & tips
  • Use path.resolve to build an absolute path to connection-org1.json so file lookup is reliable.
  • Create a filesystem wallet to manage certificates and private keys locally during development.
  • Check for the appUser identity; its absence is expected before enrollment and confirms the wallet is available.
  • Set discovery enabled and asLocalhost true for test-network local development so the Gateway can learn services dynamically.
Key Takeaway
This minimal app demonstrates loading the CCP and initializing a Gateway; resolving file paths and wallet identity checks are common early validation steps.

screens.title: Wallets and Identities
screens.narratorSegment: A wallet stores identities the client can use to authenticate to the network. The filesystem wallet implementation keeps identity credentials on disk under a folder such as wallet. Identities include an X.509 certificate and the corresponding private key provisioned by a CA. In our example app the code checks for an identity named appUser. The first run typically finds no identity and prints a message directing you to run an enrollment script. This behavior is expected and confirms the application is correctly reading the wallet. A common misconception is that the Gateway will auto-enroll users; it will not. Enrollment is a separate administrative step. screens.title: Gateway discovery options
screens.narratorSegment: When calling gateway. connect the discovery options control how the SDK learns the network topology. Setting discovery enabled to true instructs the Gateway to query peers for information about endorsing peers and orderers, which is helpful when the network topology can change. The asLocalhost option tells the SDK that endpoints in the CCP that were generated for containers or hosts should be treated as localhost for development environments — this is typical for the test-network where the certificates are generated for local use. A common mistake is leaving discovery disabled, which forces static endpoint usage and may ignore updated peer roles. Another common error is using asLocalhost true in production; that setting is explicitly for local development because it overrides hostnames in TLS validation. Concrete example: for the test-network use discovery enabled and asLocalhost true, which allows the Gateway to discover available peers and accept the test certificates bound to localhost. Key takeaway: use discovery and asLocalhost for local testing, and switch discovery and hostname options appropriately in deployed environments. Gateway discovery options means enable discovery for dynamic topology awareness and use aslocalhost only for local test setups where certificates reference localhost.. In practical terms, enabled: true and aslocalhost: true explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will prepare a practical Node. js environment for building Hyperledger Fabric client applications. You will learn which system prerequisites matter, how to initialize a Node. js project, which Hyperledger Fabric npm packages to install, and how to use a common connection profile so your client can talk to a running test-network. This setup is the foundation for every Fabric application: correct Node and npm versions avoid runtime incompatibilities, the package manifest keeps dependencies reproducible, and the connection profile tells the SDK where peers, orderers, and certificate authorities live. As a concrete example, we will load the provided connection-org1. json into a small app, initialize a Wallet, and attempt a Gateway connection. Expect to see an expected message that an application identity is missing, which confirms you loaded the profile correctly. Finally, I'll point out two frequent mistakes — wrong file paths for TLS certificates and a stopped Fabric network — and show how verifying those resolves most connection failures. After this orientation, you'll be ready to create the project scaffolding and run the sample app.

These learning objectives define practical outcomes you should achieve. First, you will identify and install the prerequisites required for Node. js Fabric development: a supported Node. js runtime and npm, and optionally a version manager such as nvm. This prevents runtime errors caused by version mismatches. Second, you will initialize and configure a Node. js project, create a package. json manifest, and add the core Hyperledger Fabric SDK packages so your code can import the Gateway and client utilities. Third, you will understand the structure of a common connection profile: how peers, orderers, certificate authorities, endpoints, and TLS certificate paths are represented. Knowing this structure helps you locate and fix path or endpoint errors. Fourth, you will establish a basic connection from a Node. js client to a running test-network by loading the CCP, creating a filesystem wallet, checking for an identity, and calling gateway. connect with discovery options. Each objective emphasizes the practical steps and why they matter. These skills let you reliably bootstrap new Fabric client projects and avoid common setup mistakes that block development.

In this page I'll translate the objectives into concrete tasks you can perform. For prerequisites, you will run the terminal commands to show the versions of Node. js and npm. This confirms compatibility and allows using nvm to switch versions when needed. For project initialization, you'll run npm init with the quick flag so a package. json is generated immediately; then you'll inspect its dependencies after installing the Fabric SDK packages. For the connection profile objective, you will open connection-org1. json and identify the peers, orderers, and tlsCACerts. path entries; understanding those fields helps you correct misconfigured endpoints. For establishing a connection, you'll run a provided app that reads the CCP, creates a filesystem wallet, and attempts gateway. connect. The expected log message about a missing identity demonstrates that the client can parse the CCP and reach the wallet logic. Each task is small and verifiable, giving you evidence that your environment is set up and ready to develop Fabric client applications.

A reliable development environment starts with the correct runtime. Node. js and npm are required because the Fabric Node. js SDK is distributed as npm packages and depends on Node's event-driven model. Use a supported LTS version to avoid incompatibilities; many Fabric SDKs are tested against recent LTS releases. To verify your environment, run the terminal checks that show the installed versions. If your version is out of range, a version manager such as nvm is a practical solution. It lets you install and switch between Node versions without interfering with system packages. For example, you might keep one LTS version for Fabric work and a different version for other projects. A common misconception is that any Node version will work; in practice, mismatched Node versions produce runtime errors or native module build failures. Another pitfall is global package pollution; prefer local project dependencies declared in package. json. Concrete example: run node -v and npm -v, then install nvm and use it to install Node 18 if your system runs an older release. Key takeaway: consistent Node and npm versions remove a large class of setup failures and make team environments reproducible.

Initializing a Node. js project produces the package. json manifest that records dependencies, scripts, and metadata. This file is critical because npm uses it to install required packages reproducibly across environments. Start by navigating to your desired project directory and running the initialization command which generates a minimal package. json. After initialization, install the core Fabric packages: hyperledger-fabric-network and hyperledger-fabric-client. Installing these populates package. json dependencies and creates node_modules. A common pitfall is installing packages globally instead of as project dependencies; global installs make it hard to reproduce the environment on other machines. Another issue is neglecting to check package-lock. json, which locks dependency versions and helps ensure that team members install the same package versions. Concrete example: run npm init -y, then npm install hyperledger-fabric-network hyperledger-fabric-client. After the install, open package. json and confirm the dependencies section includes the SDK packages. A common connection profile is the client's blueprint for reaching the Fabric network. It is a JSON or YAML file that describes the network topology from the client perspective: which peers and orderers exist, how to reach them, which certificate authorities issue identities, channel information, and timeouts. Key fields include peers, orderers, certificateAuthorities, and client settings. Each peer and orderer entry contains a URL and a tlsCACerts reference that points to a TLS root certificate file. The CCP centralizes network endpoints so client code can simply load the profile instead of hardcoding addresses. TLS certificate paths referenced inside the CCP can be relative or absolute, and the SDK resolves those paths relative to where the CCP file is loaded. An absolute path removes ambiguity but reduces portability between machines. When calling gateway. connect the discovery options control how the SDK learns the network topology. Setting discovery enabled to true instructs the Gateway to query peers for information about endorsing peers and orderers, which is helpful when the network topology can change. The asLocalhost option tells the SDK that endpoints in the CCP that were generated for containers or hosts should be treated as localhost for development environments — this is typical for the test-network where the certificates are generated for local use. A common mistake is leaving discovery disabled, which forces static endpoint usage and may ignore updated peer roles. Another common error is using asLocalhost true in production; that setting is explicitly for local development because it overrides hostnames in TLS validation.
